newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE-Japan noble family served a different court.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Japan noble family served a different court.

text.p: Born to nobility, Kimmoto Saga expected to follow a long family tradition of service in Japan's royal court.
But instead, those imperial roots threw him into the tumultuous divide between Japan and China when his sister was forced to marry Pu Jie, brother of the last emperor of China.
The Japanese military, in the midst of a campaign to conquer China in the 1930s, came up with a plot to cement ties between the two through a marriage of their royal families.

"At first the army wanted someone from the emperor's family to be his wife, but Japanese regulations forbade the Imperial family to marry foreigners. Next in line were the noble families," Saga, 75, told Reuters in an interview.
"The reason my family was chosen was because of our roots; my grandmother came from the Nakayama family and was a cousin of the Meiji emperor," Saga said.
Family patriarch Tadamitsu Nakayama was a court noble active in the movement to overthrow the Tokugawa shogunate and restore direct imperial rule in the mid-19th century.

Saga had graduated from the elite Tokyo University with a degree in Oriental Studies and planned to take a position as a chamberlain in the Imperial Household Agency, which is responsible for the affairs of the emperor and his family.
But the impending war forced him to change his plans and he became a military officer instead.
In 1931, the Japanese army, anxious to extend its hold on resource-rich Manchuria, blew up the South Manchuria Railway and blamed the incident on the Chinese.

They seized the northeastern Chinese province a year later and brought Henry Pu Yi, who had abdicated as the Qing dynasty emperor 20 years earlier, out of seclusion to become the emperor of the new puppet state of Manchukuo.
MILITARY WANTED MALE HEIR TO CHINESE THRONE
However, they found later that Pu Yi was fond of men and grew worried that he would not be able to produce an heir, Saga said.
"The army wanted Pu Jie to marry a Japanese woman and if he had a male child, they would let him take over the throne."
Despite the initial objections of Saga's family, his elder sister Hiro married Pu Jie in 1937 in Tokyo.
"The Japanese government persuaded them that this would be good for the Japanese nation, and my father reluctantly agreed. Luckily, when she met him, she liked him," Saga said.

They lived together in Chiba prefecture, near Tokyo, for less than a year before Pu Jie, who had graduated from Japan's Army Officers College, was summoned to Manchukuo to serve as a top official for the military, following Japan's full-scale invasion of China.
PU YI HATED THE JAPANESE BUT LOVED HIS FAMILY

Although Pu Yi was a willing pawn in Japan's attempt to conquer China, Saga said that Pu Yi despised the Japanese and wanted to restore his family, which had been deposed by the 1911 Nationalist revolution, to its past glory.
"He was a very cautious individual. I met him often and my impression of him was that he did not like Japanese people, but loved his family tradition. He wanted to revive that," he said.
There are many misconceptions about Pu Yi, aggravated by inaccuracies in director Bernardo Bertolucci's award-winning film, "The Last Emperor", which Saga said was "fiction".
"The director embellished many facts in the movie. Did you see my sister Hiro in the movie? Her hairstyle was like something out of Yoshiwara (a pre-war Japanese brothel district)."

Both Pu Yi and Pu Jie were imprisoned for nearly a decade following the communist revolution of 1949. Hiro returned to Japan where she spent nearly a decade teaching calligraphy at Tokyo's private Machida Gakuen high school, where Saga now is chairman.
ZHOU ENLAI PROTECTED PU YI AND PU JIE FROM HARM
Hiro was reunited with Pu Jie in the early 1960s when China was still suffering from famine after Chairman Mao Zedong's "Great Leap Forward" had pushed the economy the other way.
"(Former Chinese premier) Zhou Enlai himself invited her to come back to China. He protected not only her but Pu Yi and Pu Jie as well," Saga said.
Saga made repeated trips to Beijing to take her food, medicine and other goods that were in short supply in China, eventually visiting 103 times in all.
Conditions worsened for the couple, with the start of Mao's Cultural Revolution in the middle of that decade putting their lives in danger.

"In 1966, a terrible thing happened. The Red Guards, who were just like children, attacked their house in Beijing. They robbed them and only allowed them to use the part of the house that was necessary for daily living."
Hiro would stick with Pu Jie through war, his fall from grace in China and eventual political rehabilitation, and bear him two daughters. The marriage ended only with her death in 1987.
That same year, Pu Jie was elected to China's National People's Congress, honoured for his efforts in working to improve relations between Japan and China in the latter stages of his life.
Pu Jie died in 1994.
